items.text: UN Deputy Special Representative, Resident Coordinator ad interim and Humanitarian Coordinator Ramanathan Balakrishnan, at a high-level ministerial ad hoc committee meeting on durable solutions for displaced people in Bentiu, said persistent high water levels and a possible super El Nino could increase flood risks in the Bentiu area, and said what may have been viewed as a longer-term contingency has to be treated as an immediate preparedness priority; the article's lead says the UN warns Bentiu could face severe flooding sooner than anticipated. Kuyok Abol Kuyok, a caretaker minister speaking for the humanitarian affairs minister, cited recurrent flooding, limited financial resources and inadequate resilient infrastructure among the challenges and called for investment in drainage, raised roads and flood protection (county inferred from Bentiu).

The South Sudan Meteorological Service's forecast for 20 to 28 October covers areas including Lainya, Yei, Morobo and Kajo-Keji in Central Equatoria; it expects moderate rainfall of 50 to 100 mm in parts of several states, including Eastern Equatoria, and of the Pibor Administrative Area, and warns communities and road users in heavier-rainfall areas to remain alert to the possibility of waterlogging, localized flooding and road or bridge damage or disruption.

UK Ambassador Rebecca Fabrizi announced an extra 2.35 million pounds to reduce El Nino-linked risks in South Sudan; the article also cites a FEWS NET report that warns El Nino-related rainfall deficits could reduce the 2026 harvest and widen food gaps, and that identifies Jonglei and southern Upper Nile as areas where the combined effects of climate shocks and conflict could have particularly severe consequences.

Emmanuel Majok Brown, chairperson of the Mvolo Cooperative Union, says farmers in Mvolo County face widespread crop losses after too little rain in May and June, including a June dry spell that reportedly lasted one to one and a half months, and warns that famine could hit the area in the next few months; he says households have used up last year's food stocks and that limited maize arriving from parts of Mundri County may not meet local demand.

Lakes State caretaker governor Rin Tueny Mabor, speaking in Rumbek, warned of possible hunger, saying May and June rainfall was insufficient for cultivation and rains that began in October came too late for this year's farming season; he said northern parts of the state were facing serious water and pasture shortages that could force cattle keepers to move herds towards southern Lakes and neighbouring areas (county not stated for the shortages).

WFP's Matthew Hollingworth says the agency faces an $86 million funding gap now and a further $416 million gap over the next six months, and warns that more than one million vulnerable people could lose access to lifesaving food and nutrition assistance by October unless additional funding is secured; he says 7.8 million people struggle to find food each day as South Sudan faces conflict, displacement, economic hardship and climate shocks. At Canal Pigi in Jonglei he met families whose farmland remained submerged seven years after the original floods, while drought affects limited areas of cultivable land.

UNMISS says heavy rains and insecurity have left communities in Ibba County even more isolated than before; the article says large sections of the roughly 100 km Yambio-Ibba road are badly damaged with deep potholes, mud and flooding, and the Ibba county chief says the situation along the road is affecting the community greatly because it is their lifeline.

In a precautionary notice, the Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation warns of possible Nile flooding in vulnerable areas in and around Juba: hydrological simulations suggest Lake Victoria could rise significantly, potentially above its historical maximum, and the notice cites ICPAC's outlook of a higher El Nino likelihood with above-normal rainfall expected over the Lake Victoria basin and parts of the wider Nile basin. Stations from Nimule to Renk and Nasir to Bentiu are currently recording decreasing levels that remain below flood-alert levels, and the article refers to the possibility of higher flows in the coming days. Reduced June-September rainfall has also affected several states and the administrative areas of Abyei, Pibor and Ruweng.

Flooding has submerged about 70% of the land in Bentiu, and the dykes built and maintained around the clock by UNMISS and IOM protect 300,000 civilians. UNMISS's Bentiu field office head estimates that 50,000 people would be submerged if UN and IOM work were affected and a dyke breach were not repaired within ten hours, and says IOM faces a shortage of resources for dyke maintenance and pumping; he expects heavy rain with El Nino from October to February (county inferred from Bentiu).
